patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Black, tarry stools for 2 days and dizziness on standing
background: NSTEMI with a drug-eluting coronary stent 5 months ago
Aspirin 75 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg daily (dual antiplatelet therapy)
Omeprazole 20 mg started by his GP 2 months ago for indigestion
Knee osteoarthritis; buys ibuprofen over the counter

diagnosis.exam: Expect a patient on aspirin or clopidogrel with melaena, haematemesis or unexplained hypotension: the answer is a GI (usually peptic ulcer) bleed. Also expect named side effects: TTP with clopidogrel, asthma and dyspepsia with aspirin.

points: Desmond, 71, has passed **black, sticky, foul-smelling stools** for 2 days.
He felt faint getting off the sofa this morning.
Weeks of **burning upper abdominal pain** after meals.
Takes aspirin, clopidogrel and over-the-counter ibuprofen.

steps.lead: Desmond's two drugs both **stop platelets sticking together**: good for his stent, bad for any ulcer that starts to bleed.
Desmond is the typical user: **ischaemic heart disease with a coronary stent**, so he is on two antiplatelets at once.

visual.title: Where Desmond's pain is
visual.caption: Epigastric burning after meals: dyspepsia from aspirin (and ibuprofen) suggests a peptic ulcer as the bleeding source.

steps.lead: Desmond has **major** bleeding: melaena with a fast pulse and low BP. His gums bleed when brushing too, the **minor** end of the spectrum.

steps.q: Desmond is on aspirin and clopidogrel, has melaena and BP 98/60. What is the most likely problem?
o: Upper GI bleed from a peptic ulcer
steps.r: **Melaena** means upper GI blood digested on its way down. Aspirin plus an NSAID and dyspepsia point to a **peptic ulcer**.

steps.lead: This is the signature picture: antiplatelet patient plus **melaena and hypotension** equals a GI bleed until proven otherwise.
Desmond's indigestion is the **aspirin GI irritation**; his GP's omeprazole may be weakening his **clopidogrel** via CYP2C19.

steps.text: Do not blame a low platelet count. On antiplatelets the **platelet count is normal**; it is platelet **function** that fails. A low count with fever and confusion on clopidogrel suggests **TTP**.
Aspirin side effects to name: **dyspepsia and peptic ulcer**, worsening of **aspirin-sensitive asthma**, and renal effects. Clopidogrel's rare serious one: **TTP**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (FBC for the Hb) and 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (endoscopy for a suspected GI bleed). A normal clotting screen is the classic finding.

steps.q: Desmond is being cannulated. Which blood test first shows how much he has bled?
steps.r: The **FBC** gives the haemoglobin, the measure of overt or occult blood loss. Clotting is usually normal on antiplatelets.

steps.lead: Desmond's **FBC** is the first-line test: his Hb shows how much he has lost.

steps.title: Desmond's bloods on arrival
steps.text: Low Hb, **normal platelets and normal clotting**, and a urea raised out of proportion to creatinine (digested blood): an upper GI bleed.

visual.title: Desmond's haemoglobin
visual.label: Desmond 82
visual.caption: Well below normal after 2 days of melaena; recheck after resuscitation as Hb lags behind acute loss.

steps.lead: Desmond's normal INR and APTT fit **antiplatelet** bleeding. A raised INR would point to warfarin instead.

points: Two large-bore cannulas; group and crossmatch sent.
BP improves to 112/70 mmHg after fluids.
Gastroenterology book him for endoscopy within 24 hours.

steps.lead: Desmond's **endoscopy** finds a duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel and treats it in the same session.

steps.text: Endoscopy is both the **gold-standard test** and the **treatment** for a suspected GI bleed: it localises the source and stops it.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (assess severity and resuscitate, then stop the antiplatelet) and timing questions: clopidogrel stops 7 days before surgery, warfarin 5 days.

steps.q: Desmond arrived with melaena, pulse 108 and BP 98/60. What comes first?
steps.r: **Assess severity first**: ABC, IV access, fluids and blood if needed. Endoscopy follows once he is resuscitated.

steps.lead: Desmond's severity was assessed first (shocked, Hb 82), then his **antiplatelets were withheld**.

steps.title: Bleeding on an antiplatelet
nodes: Resuscitate: IV fluids, transfuse if severe
Treat the source (endoscopy for GI bleed)
Weigh bleeding vs stent thrombosis before restarting
steps.caption: Severity first, then stop the drug, then fix the source.

steps.lead: Desmond's ulcer was clipped at endoscopy. With a **5-month-old stent**, cardiology weigh his thrombosis risk before restarting.

steps.text: Do not just leave a stent patient off all antiplatelets. Stopping too long risks **stent thrombosis**; the restart decision balances both risks.
Desmond's omeprazole is swapped for **lansoprazole** (MHRA advice): omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit **CYP2C19** and weaken clopidogrel. His ibuprofen is stopped.

visual.title: Stop before elective surgery (days)
visual.label: Clopidogrel 7 days
visual.caption: Clopidogrel stops 7 days before surgery; warfarin 5 days, with LMWH cover.

steps.lead: If Desmond later needs his knee replaced, **clopidogrel stops 7 days** before. Warfarin rules are shown for comparison.
Desmond's plan follows **NICE CKS: Antiplatelet treatment**.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why aspirin's effect lasts a week, why clopidogrel fails with omeprazole, why clotting tests stay normal, and why aspirin causes ulcers.

steps.lead: Desmond's aspirin **permanently acetylates COX-1**, so each platelet stays inhibited for its whole life.

steps.title: Aspirin in the platelet
nodes: Lasts the platelet lifespan, about 7–10 days

visual.title: Platelet function after Desmond's last aspirin
visual.caption: Recovery tracks new platelet production from the marrow, not drug clearance.

steps.lead: Desmond's clopidogrel is a **prodrug**; his omeprazole blocks the **CYP2C19** step that activates it.

steps.q: Why might Desmond's omeprazole have put his stent at risk?
o: It inhibits CYP2C19, reducing clopidogrel activation
It raises gastric pH, blocking aspirin absorption
steps.r: Omeprazole and esomeprazole **inhibit CYP2C19**, so less active clopidogrel metabolite is made and **P2Y12** blockade is weaker.

steps.lead: Desmond's INR and APTT were normal because the **cascade** is intact; his platelets just cannot aggregate.
Had Desmond come in confused with purpura and low platelets, **clopidogrel-associated TTP** would be the worry.
Desmond's ulcer came from losing **gastroprotective prostaglandins** (COX-1), worsened by his ibuprofen.

mcq.q: Which rare haematological complication is associated with clopidogrel?
mcq.r: **TTP** is a rare but serious complication of thienopyridines such as clopidogrel.

mcq.q: Which is a recognised side effect of aspirin?
mcq.r: Aspirin can worsen **aspirin-sensitive asthma**; it also causes dyspepsia, PUD and renal effects.

mcq.q: What is the platelet count usually like in a patient bleeding on antiplatelets?
mcq.r: The count is usually **normal**; platelet **function** is impaired.

mcq.q: Which is the first-line investigation for suspected blood loss on antiplatelets?
mcq.r: **FBC** shows the Hb for occult or overt blood loss.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard investigation for a suspected GI bleed on aspirin?
What does the coagulation profile typically show on antiplatelets?
mcq.r: Antiplatelets affect platelet function, not the cascade, so PT/APTT/INR are **normal**.

mcq.q: How many days before elective surgery should clopidogrel be stopped?
mcq.r: **7 days**; warfarin is stopped 5 days before.

mcq.q: What is the first step when a patient on antiplatelets presents with bleeding?
mcq.r: **Assess severity first**, then stop the antiplatelet.
Clopidogrel irreversibly blocks the platelet **P2Y12 ADP receptor**.

mcq.q: Why does aspirin's antiplatelet effect last 7 to 10 days?
o: It irreversibly inhibits COX-1 in platelets
mcq.r: COX-1 is **irreversibly acetylated** and platelets cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts their lifespan.

prompts.q: What do antiplatelet drugs do, who takes them, and what is the trade-off?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name both drugs and the reason the patient is on them.

points.p: Aspirin and clopidogrel inhibit platelet aggregation
points.why: They act on platelets, not the clotting cascade.

points.p: Reduce clot formation but increase bleeding risk
points.why: This trade-off drives every restart decision.

points.p: Used in cardiovascular disease, previous MI or stroke, after a coronary stent
points.why: A stent stem means dual antiplatelet therapy and higher bleeding risk.

prompts.q: How does bleeding on antiplatelets present? Give minor and major examples and the signs of significant bleeding.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: grade the bleed before you act.

points.p: Minor: bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding
points.why: Minor bleeding rarely needs the drug stopped urgently.

points.p: Major: GI bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage
points.why: Major bleeds are the ones that kill.

points.p: Haematuria and prolonged bleeding also occur
points.why: Any site can bleed.

points.p: Significant bleeding: hypotension, pallor if anaemic
points.why: Hypotension is the signature 'unexplained' clue.

prompts.q: What is the signature presentation that should make you think of a GI bleed on antiplatelets?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three triggers in a stem with aspirin or clopidogrel.

points.p: Melaena
points.why: Black tarry stool means upper GI blood.

points.p: Haematemesis
points.why: Coffee-ground or fresh blood vomit.

points.p: Unexplained hypotension
points.why: Bleeding can be occult before melaena appears.

prompts.q: List the side effects of aspirin and the key complication and interaction of clopidogrel.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'which side effect' question often hides asthma or TTP.

points.p: Aspirin: GI irritation, dyspepsia, peptic ulcer disease
points.why: Due to loss of gastroprotective prostaglandins.

points.p: Aspirin: exacerbates aspirin-sensitive asthma
points.why: Look for nasal polyps or new wheeze after starting aspirin.

points.p: Aspirin: renal effects
points.why: Prostaglandin loss reduces renal blood flow.

points.p: Clopidogrel: rare but serious TTP
points.why: Low platelets, haemolysis, fever, confusion, renal impairment.

points.p: Omeprazole/esomeprazole reduce clopidogrel efficacy
points.why: Via CYP2C19; lansoprazole or pantoprazole are preferred.

prompts.q: What is the first-line test, the gold-standard test, and the typical clotting result in antiplatelet bleeding?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'initial' and 'diagnostic' have different answers.

points.p: First-line: FBC for Hb
points.why: Shows occult or overt blood loss.

points.p: Gold standard: endoscopy if GI bleed suspected
points.why: Localises and treats the source.

points.p: Coagulation profile typically normal
points.why: Helps distinguish antiplatelet from anticoagulant bleeding.

prompts.q: What are the steps in managing bleeding on an antiplatelet, and what decides when to restart?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: severity first, then stop the drug, then the source.

points.p: Assess severity of bleeding first
points.why: The ordered first step in the notes.

points.p: Then stop the antiplatelet
points.why: Comes after the severity assessment.

points.p: Treat the source: endoscopy for GI bleed
points.why: Endoscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.

points.p: Resuscitate severe bleeds: IV fluids, transfusion
points.why: Platelet count is normal, so this is not about platelets.

points.p: Balance bleeding risk against thrombosis risk before restarting
points.why: A recent stent makes stopping dangerous.

prompts.q: When are clopidogrel and warfarin stopped before surgery, and how is warfarin reversed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 7 versus 5 days is a classic swap.

points.p: Clopidogrel stopped 7 days before surgery
points.why: Matches the 7 to 10 day platelet lifespan.

points.p: Warfarin stopped 5 days before, LMWH cover
points.why: Bridging protects high thrombotic risk patients.

points.p: Reversal: stop warfarin, 5 mg IV vitamin K, recheck INR at 12 hours (below 1.5)
points.why: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not antiplatelets.

prompts.q: How do aspirin and clopidogrel inhibit platelets, and why does omeprazole interact with clopidogrel?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the enzyme, the receptor and the CYP.

points.p: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2
points.why: Thromboxane A2 drives aggregation.

points.p: Effect lasts the platelet lifespan, about 7–10 days
points.why: Platelets have no nucleus to make new COX-1.

points.p: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that irreversibly blocks P2Y12 ADP receptor
points.why: Different target from aspirin, so the two add together.

points.p: Activated by hepatic CYP2C19, inhibited by omeprazole/esomeprazole
points.why: Less active drug means more stent thrombosis.

prompts.q: Why do clotting tests stay normal, why does clopidogrel cause TTP, and why does aspirin cause ulcers?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the finding in the stem.

points.p: Antiplatelets impair platelet function, not the coagulation cascade, so PT/APTT/INR stay normal
points.why: Normal clotting does not mean low bleeding risk.

points.p: TTP linked to ADAMTS13 deficiency causing microvascular platelet thrombi
points.why: Thienopyridines: clopidogrel and ticlopidine.

points.p: COX-1 inhibition reduces gastroprotective prostaglandins
points.why: Explains dyspepsia and peptic ulceration.

glossary.antiplatelet: A drug that stops platelets sticking together, reducing arterial clots but increasing bleeding.
glossary.aspirin: Antiplatelet that irreversibly blocks COX-1, stopping thromboxane A2 production.
glossary.clopidogrel: Antiplatelet prodrug that irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor.
glossary.DAPT: Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, usually after a coronary stent or ACS.
glossary.COX-1: Cyclooxygenase-1: enzyme that makes thromboxane in platelets and protective prostaglandins in the stomach.
glossary.COX-2: Inducible cyclooxygenase involved in inflammation; also blocked by aspirin.
glossary.thromboxane A2: Platelet-made signal that causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.
glossary.P2Y12: Platelet ADP receptor whose activation drives aggregation; the target of clopidogrel and ticagrelor.
glossary.ADP: Adenosine diphosphate: released by activated platelets to recruit more platelets.
glossary.prodrug: A drug given in inactive form that the body must convert to its active metabolite.
glossary.CYP2C19: Liver enzyme that activates clopidogrel; inhibited by omeprazole and esomeprazole.
glossary.omeprazole: Proton pump inhibitor that inhibits CYP2C19 and so reduces clopidogrel's effect.
glossary.lansoprazole: Proton pump inhibitor preferred with clopidogrel because it interacts less via CYP2C19.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor: reduces stomach acid; used to protect against and treat ulcers.
glossary.melaena: Black, tarry, foul-smelling stool from digested blood, usually an upper GI bleed.
glossary.haematemesis: Vomiting blood, fresh red or coffee-ground.
glossary.dyspepsia: Indigestion: upper abdominal burning or discomfort, often after meals.
glossary.PUD: Peptic ulcer disease: ulcers of the stomach or duodenum.
glossary.peptic ulcer: A break in the stomach or duodenal lining; aspirin and NSAIDs are common causes.
glossary.TTP: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: microvascular platelet clots causing low platelets, haemolysis, fever, confusion and renal impairment.
glossary.ADAMTS13: Enzyme that cleaves von Willebrand factor; deficiency causes TTP.
glossary.thienopyridines: Class of P2Y12 blockers including clopidogrel and ticlopidine.
glossary.schistocytes: Fragmented red cells on a blood film, seen in microangiopathic haemolysis such as TTP.
glossary.endoscopy: Camera test of the gut; for a GI bleed it finds and treats the bleeding point.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio: standardised prothrombin time used to monitor warfarin.
glossary.APTT: Activated partial thromboplastin time: tests the intrinsic clotting pathway.
glossary.PT: Prothrombin time: tests the extrinsic clotting pathway.
glossary.coagulation cascade: Chain of clotting factor reactions that makes fibrin; untouched by antiplatelets.
glossary.LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, e.g. enoxaparin; used to bridge when warfarin is stopped.
glossary.vitamin K: Restores clotting factors II, VII, IX and X; reverses warfarin.
glossary.warfarin: Oral anticoagulant that blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; raises the INR.
glossary.stent thrombosis: Clot forming inside a coronary stent, causing MI; the danger of stopping antiplatelets early.
glossary.aspirin-sensitive asthma: Asthma worsened by aspirin and NSAIDs, often with nasal polyps.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, e.g. ibuprofen; adds GI bleeding risk with aspirin.
glossary.Glasgow-Blatchford score: Risk score for upper GI bleeding using urea, Hb, BP, pulse and other features.

technique.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 3 month history of tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. She had an ischaemic stroke 2 years ago and takes aspirin 75 mg daily. She also takes naproxen for hip pain and has had burning epigastric pain after meals. Her stools are dark. She looks pale.
technique.q: Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?

steps.x: A cause question: find the source of a microcytic anaemia in someone on aspirin.
Aspirin plus an NSAID damage the stomach lining; dyspepsia and dark stools point to an **upper GI** source; low MCV means iron loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic upper GI blood loss from an aspirin and NSAID ulcer: a **bleeding peptic ulcer**.

elim: Anaemia of chronic disease is usually normocytic with no dark stools.
Colorectal cancer is possible but dark stools with epigastric dyspepsia on aspirin favour an upper source.
Platelets are normal.
B12 deficiency gives a high MCV.

steps.x: **B. Bleeding peptic ulcer.** Rule: aspirin + dyspepsia + dark stools = upper GI bleed until endoscopy says otherwise.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a 2 day history of black stools. He had a coronary stent inserted 3 months ago and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. After 1 litre of intravenous fluid his pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. His haemoglobin is 96 g/L.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' means the gold standard that confirms the source.
Melaena with a raised urea is an **upper GI** bleed; he is now resuscitated and stable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Upper GI endoscopy**: it localises and treats the bleed.

elim: Clotting is usually normal on antiplatelets; it does not find the source.
Colonoscopy looks at the lower GI tract; melaena is upper.
CT angiography is for active bleeding when endoscopy fails or is not possible.
FIT is a screening test for occult blood, not an acute bleed.

steps.x: **E. Upper GI endoscopy.** Rule: suspected GI bleed on antiplatelets, endoscopy is gold standard.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man has had bleeding gums when brushing his teeth and easy bruising on his arms for 2 months. He had a coronary stent inserted for unstable angina 18 months ago and still takes aspirin 75 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg daily. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Refer for urgent upper GI endoscopy

steps.x: A management step after the bleeding has been assessed.
**Minor** bleeding with normal Hb and obs; dual therapy has run well past the usual **12 months** after a stent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Severity assessed (minor), so stop the antiplatelet he no longer needs: **stop clopidogrel**, keep aspirin for secondary prevention.

elim: He has troublesome bleeding and no longer needs two agents.
His platelet count is normal and the bleeding is minor.
No GI symptoms and a normal Hb; nothing to scope.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not antiplatelets.

steps.x: **E. Stop clopidogrel and continue aspirin.** Rule: assess severity, then stop the antiplatelet, balancing thrombosis risk.

technique.stem: A 63 year old man is admitted with a myocardial infarction 4 months after a coronary stent was inserted. Angiography shows stent thrombosis. He takes aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin and omeprazole, which was started 3 months ago for indigestion. He says he has taken every dose.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his stent thrombosis?
o: Reduced activation of clopidogrel by CYP2C19

steps.x: A mechanism question: why did his antiplatelet therapy fail?
Good adherence, so it is a drug interaction: omeprazole with clopidogrel.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Omeprazole inhibits **CYP2C19**, so the clopidogrel prodrug is not activated and P2Y12 is not blocked.

elim: Aspirin is not cleared this way and PPIs do not induce CYP3A4.
Absorption is not the problem; activation is.
Statins do not affect aspirin's COX-1 acetylation.
Receptor upregulation is not the recognised mechanism.

steps.x: **C. Reduced activation of clopidogrel by CYP2C19.** Use lansoprazole or pantoprazole instead.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting dark brown material twice. He takes aspirin 75 mg daily after a myocardial infarction and ibuprofen for back pain. He has had epigastric discomfort for a month. His pulse rate is 114 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Coffee-ground haematemesis, shock and a raised urea on aspirin plus an NSAID with prior dyspepsia is a bleeding peptic ulcer. Varices need liver disease; Mallory-Weiss follows repeated retching.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an upper GI bleed in a patient on aspirin.
Coffee-ground haematemesis, aspirin + NSAID, dyspepsia and **hypotension**: the signature antiplatelet GI bleed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bleeding peptic ulcer** from aspirin and NSAID mucosal damage.

elim: Boerhaave causes chest pain and surgical emphysema after vomiting, not haematemesis.
Gastric cancer gives weight loss and slow bleeding, not acute shock.
Mallory-Weiss follows forceful retching; there is no such history.
Varices need cirrhosis or portal hypertension, not given.

steps.x: **A. Bleeding peptic ulcer.** Antiplatelet + haematemesis + hypotension = GI bleed.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has noticed large bruises on her arms and legs after minor knocks for 6 weeks. Clopidogrel was started 2 months ago after a transient ischaemic attack. She is otherwise well and takes no other medicines. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bruising?
practice.e: Easy bruising on clopidogrel with a normal platelet count and normal clotting is impaired platelet function. ITP needs a low count; vitamin K deficiency raises the INR.

steps.x: Cause of bruising: decide whether the problem is count, function or cascade.

clues: bruises on her arms and legs after minor knocks
steps.x: New bruising after starting clopidogrel, otherwise well; the labs show a **normal count** and **normal clotting**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clopidogrel blocks P2Y12, so platelets are there but do not work: **impaired platelet function**.

elim: Leukaemia gives cytopenias; her count and Hb are normal.
Haemophilia A prolongs the APTT and starts in childhood.
ITP means a low platelet count.
Vitamin K deficiency raises the INR.

steps.x: **D. Impaired platelet function.** Rule: antiplatelet bleeding has a normal count and normal clotting.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man is brought in with confusion and fever for 2 days. He started clopidogrel 3 weeks ago after a coronary stent. He has petechiae on his legs. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg. A blood film shows schistocytes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, confusion, renal impairment, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis weeks after starting clopidogrel is TTP. DIC prolongs the clotting times; HUS follows bloody diarrhoea.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a low platelet count, which antiplatelets alone do not cause.
Fever, confusion, petechiae, fragmented red cells; labs add low platelets, raised creatinine and a **normal INR**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clopidogrel's rare serious complication: **TTP** (ADAMTS13 deficiency, microvascular platelet thrombi).

elim: DIC consumes clotting factors, so the INR would be raised.
HUS usually follows E. coli bloody diarrhoea and is renal-dominant.
HIT needs heparin exposure 5 to 10 days earlier.
ITP does not cause haemolysis, fever or confusion.

steps.x: **E. TTP.** Clopidogrel + low platelets + schistocytes + confusion = TTP, a haematological emergency.

practice.stem: A 56 year old woman has a 1 week history of wheeze and breathlessness. She has asthma and nasal polyps. Aspirin 75 mg was started 10 days ago after a myocardial infarction. She has no fever or ankle swelling. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There is widespread expiratory wheeze.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
practice.e: Wheeze starting days after aspirin in an asthmatic with nasal polyps is aspirin-sensitive asthma, a recognised aspirin side effect. No crackles, oedema or fever to suggest failure or pneumonia.

steps.x: A cause question: link the new symptom to the new drug.

clues: Aspirin 75 mg was started 10 days ago
steps.x: Asthma + polyps + new aspirin + wheeze: the classic aspirin-sensitive pattern.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspirin-sensitive asthma** exacerbated by her new antiplatelet.

elim: Heart failure would give crackles and oedema; ankles are clear.
Pneumonia needs fever and focal signs.
Pericarditis causes pleuritic chest pain, not wheeze.
PE gives sudden breathlessness and hypoxia, not wheeze.

steps.x: **B. Aspirin-sensitive asthma.** Remember the aspirin side effects: GI, asthma, renal.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man on aspirin and clopidogrel after a coronary stent has had nosebleeds lasting 20 minutes on three occasions this month. He takes no other medicines. He is well between episodes. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely result on his blood tests?
o: Low platelet count with normal INR
Normal platelet count with normal INR
Normal platelet count with prolonged APTT
Normal platelet count with raised INR
practice.e: Antiplatelets impair platelet function, not number or the cascade, so the count and clotting tests are normal. A raised INR suggests warfarin; a prolonged APTT suggests heparin or haemophilia.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question about antiplatelet bleeding.
Prolonged epistaxis on two antiplatelets and nothing else: a platelet **function** problem.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Normal platelet count and normal clotting**.

elim: That is DIC, a consumptive coagulopathy.
Antiplatelets do not lower the count (TTP is rare and he is well).
APTT is not affected by antiplatelets.
A raised INR suggests warfarin or liver disease.

steps.x: **C. Normal platelet count with normal INR.** Normal tests do not mean normal bleeding risk.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has central chest pain for 1 hour. He had a drug-eluting coronary stent inserted 6 weeks ago and takes aspirin and clopidogrel, which he never misses. His GP started esomeprazole 4 weeks ago for heartburn. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 142/88 mmHg. Angiography shows thrombosis within the stent.

visual.title: Stent thrombosis on angiography
visual.caption: Occlusion inside the recently stented LAD.

practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his stent thrombosis?
practice.e: Esomeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, reducing activation of the clopidogrel prodrug, so platelets are less inhibited. He is adherent and there is no heparin exposure.

steps.x: Cause of antiplatelet failure in an adherent patient.

clues: aspirin and clopidogrel, which he never misses
steps.x: New PPI that interacts with clopidogrel, then stent thrombosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **drug interaction**: esomeprazole blocks CYP2C19 activation of clopidogrel.

elim: Dyspepsia does not cause aspirin resistance.
There is no heparin exposure or low platelet count.
He never misses a dose.
TTP causes low platelets and haemolysis, not a single stent clot.

steps.x: **B. Drug interaction reducing clopidogrel effect.** Avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole with clopidogrel.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman takes aspirin 75 mg daily after a stroke. She has felt increasingly tired for 2 months and her daughter says she looks pale. She has occasional indigestion but no visible bleeding. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 124/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: The FBC is first-line: the Hb shows occult blood loss on aspirin. Endoscopy is the gold standard once a GI bleed is suspected, not the first test; clotting is usually normal.

steps.x: 'Initial' investigation: the first, simplest test.
Possible **occult** blood loss on aspirin: you need the Hb.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **FBC** for haemoglobin.

elim: Clotting is usually normal on antiplatelets.
CT is not a first-line test for anaemia.
Platelet function tests do not show blood loss.
Endoscopy is the gold standard, done after the FBC confirms anaemia.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count.** Initial = FBC; diagnostic = endoscopy.

practice.stem: An 80 year old man is brought from a care home with extensive bruising and a nosebleed. He has atrial fibrillation and ischaemic heart disease, and his medication chart is missing. Staff think he takes either warfarin or clopidogrel. His pulse rate is 84 bpm, irregularly irregular, and BP 130/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which investigation would best distinguish between the two drugs as the cause?
practice.e: The coagulation profile is typically normal on antiplatelets but the INR is raised on warfarin, so it separates antiplatelet from anticoagulant bleeding. The platelet count is normal with both.

steps.x: Which test separates antiplatelet from anticoagulant bleeding?
Either drug could cause the bleeding, and the platelet count is normal: you need a test of the **cascade**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coagulation profile**: normal on clopidogrel, raised INR on warfarin.

elim: A film does not measure drug effect.
D-dimer is for clots, not drug effect.
Fibrinogen is normal with both drugs.
He already has an FBC; the count is normal with both.

steps.x: **B. Coagulation profile (INR).** Normal clotting with bleeding points to the antiplatelet.

practice.stem: A 65 year old woman is admitted with haematemesis. She takes aspirin 75 mg daily for ischaemic heart disease. She is pale and clammy. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. She has two large-bore cannulas in place.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Intravenous fluid resuscitation and crossmatch blood
practice.e: She is shocked from a major GI bleed, so assess severity and resuscitate with IV fluids and blood first. Endoscopy follows resuscitation; vitamin K reverses warfarin, not aspirin.

steps.x: 'Initial' management in a shocked bleeding patient.
Major bleed with **shock** and Hb 71: severe.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Resuscitate: **IV fluids and blood**.

elim: Vitamin K reverses warfarin; her INR is normal.
Platelet count is normal; transfusion is not first.
Tranexamic acid is not recommended in upper GI bleeding.
Endoscopy comes once she is resuscitated.

steps.x: **A. IV fluid resuscitation and crossmatch.** Severity first, resuscitate, then stop aspirin and scope.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man is listed for an elective laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair in 3 weeks. He takes clopidogrel 75 mg daily after an ischaemic stroke 2 years ago. He has no coronary stent. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about his clopidogrel?
practice.e: The standard perioperative recommendation is to stop clopidogrel 7 days before surgery, matching the platelet lifespan. Five days is the warfarin rule.

steps.x: A timing question about stopping an antiplatelet before surgery.
Elective surgery, single antiplatelet, no stent: follow the standard rule.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **7 days** before surgery.

elim: Continuing raises surgical bleeding risk with no stent to protect.
One day is far too short; the effect lasts the platelet lifespan.
Three days is too short.
Five days is the warfarin rule.

steps.x: **E. Stop 7 days before surgery.** Clopidogrel 7, warfarin 5.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man had a coronary stent inserted 2 months ago and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He has had heartburn and epigastric discomfort for 3 weeks. He has no weight loss, dysphagia or vomiting. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. His GP decides to start a proton pump inhibitor.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate proton pump inhibitor?
practice.e: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and reduce clopidogrel's effect, so lansoprazole (or pantoprazole) is preferred. He needs gastroprotection on dual antiplatelets with dyspepsia.

steps.x: Choose the PPI that is safe with clopidogrel.
Dyspepsia on dual antiplatelets needs a PPI that does not block clopidogrel activation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lansoprazole** (or pantoprazole).

elim: Esomeprazole inhibits CYP2C19.
He is symptomatic on two antiplatelets and needs protection.
Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19.
Still contains omeprazole; ranitidine is withdrawn in the UK.

steps.x: **B. Lansoprazole.** Rule: avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole with clopidogrel.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man stops aspirin before a dental extraction. He took his last dose 2 days ago. The dentist notes that his bleeding time is still prolonged, although aspirin has a plasma half-life of under 1 hour.
practice.q: Which best explains why aspirin's effect persists?
o: Aspirin is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19
practice.e: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, and platelets cannot make new enzyme, so thromboxane A2 production stays blocked for the platelet lifespan of 7 to 10 days. P2Y12 and CYP2C19 describe clopidogrel.

steps.x: Mechanism: why the effect outlasts the drug.
Short half-life, long effect: the drug must act **irreversibly** on a cell that cannot repair itself.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Irreversible COX-1 acetylation** in anucleate platelets.

elim: Aspirin does not accumulate in fat.
P2Y12 is clopidogrel's target.
That is clopidogrel's activation.
Antiplatelets do not affect the PT.

steps.x: **B. Irreversible acetylation of platelet COX-1.** Effect lasts 7 to 10 days.
